settles and giving up after ten minutes.

While a build runs the card says Deploying, with a bar sweeping across its
top edge and a ping on the status dot. The pill's old fade was a six-pixel

Deploying also overrides health, because the API only moves health off
not_deployed once the allocation exists, which is well after the point where
somebody is watching.

A failed poll keeps the cards it has: one blip mid-build is not a reason to
replace the grid with an error.

minutes later with an error that names something else. Both are knowable in
the browser, so check for them right after packing and offer the folder to

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Stop opening the docs with "get a deploy token"
commits.body:
Anonymous deploys have always worked, but every path through the docs led with
a credential: Quick start's step 1 was "Get a deploy token", Authentication
said deploys are "authenticated one of two ways" and put tokens first, and
every curl example carried an Authorization header whether or not the call
needed one. An agent reading that reasonably concludes it must get the user a
token before it can do anything — which turns a one-minute trial into a signup
before there is even an app to look at.

The order now matches what the platform actually requires. Quick start
deploys with no credential and polls with no credential, and claiming the app
is step 3, explicitly worth doing later rather than first. Authentication says
plainly that omitting the header is a first-class path, not a degraded one,
and tells an agent to show the URL before raising the subject. The token
section now opens by naming what needs one, and the examples that keep their
header say where to drop it.

The hackathon page had the same problem by implication — participants deploy
before a token exists, and the event code is about Pro, not permission.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Check an app name against the rules that actually apply
commits.body:
The upload accepted names the deploy endpoint won't. Its `limits` block also
sets a minimum of 3 characters, a maximum of 63, and reserves some names —
`docs`, `api`, `www` and others — none of which were checked here, so "ab" or
an app called "docs" was packed, uploaded, and only then refused.

The rules now live in one place, mirrored from capabilities, and are applied
under the field as it's typed as well as in the route, because a limit the
browser enforces is a courtesy rather than a control. A redeploy's name came
from the platform, so it is never presented as the uploader's to fix.

The reserved list is `reserved_examples` upstream — longer than what it names —
so a rejection from the endpoint stays authoritative.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Stop calling it copying a prompt
commits.body:
Copying a prompt became one of two ways through that button when the upload tab
landed, so the label named a mechanism the reader might not use, and both
dialogs still described only the paste route. All three say what happens now
instead: ship a new version, by whichever means.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Let people deploy an app without going through an agent
commits.body:
Handing the agent a prompt stays the default, and is still the path that keeps
working afterwards — the agent that deployed can also fix and redeploy. But
someone who already has the app built had no way in at all, so "Deploy an app"
now has a second tab: drop a folder or a zip.

The endpoint takes one thing, a gzipped tar posted as multipart source, so the
browser converts to that before anything is sent. A zip is unpacked and
repacked; a tarball is passed through untouched. Both directions are native —
CompressionStream and DecompressionStream — because a packing library would be
shipped to every visitor for a screen most of them never open.

The upload can't go straight to the deploy endpoint from the page: the session
is an httpOnly cookie, so only the server can read the PAT to sign with. Hence
the route, which is also why /api/apps/[slug]/logs exists. The PAT is sent with
an X-Company-Id rather than swapped for a deploy token first — a deploy token
is a long-lived company-wide secret, and one should only exist because somebody
asked for one to use outside the browser.

Packing happens on drop rather than on Deploy, so the name and the file count
are on screen before anything…

matched nothing, and the active tab lost its underline. And the /alpha suffixes
are gone: the palette is var()-based, so text-foreground/60 renders nothing at
all, the trap ProjectAnalytics already documents.

There is no /login route — signing in happens in a modal — but both the docs
and llms.txt opened the token instructions with "go to embarko.ai/login",
which 404s. That is step one of getting a deploy token, so it is the first
thing a new user or an agent acting for one actually tries.

/app/tokens prompts for sign-in by itself, so the two steps collapse into one.

The sitemap also advertised /showcase/submit to search engines. Submitting
moved into the console at /app/showcase/submit when it grew a page there, and
every link in the app already points at the new one; only the sitemap entry
was left behind, pointing at a 404. Removed rather than repointed, since the
console is signed-in and deliberately out of the sitemap.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Keep the old troubleshooting address working
commits.body:
Moving these two docs under /docs left their old addresses dead, which was
the intent at the time — the project is new and the links were assumed to be
ours to break. They turned out not to be. The capabilities manifest the deploy
host serves to agents names /troubleshoot, and so does the deploy script
people have already installed, which prints it in the error output of a
failed deploy.

Both are out of reach of a site change and neither can be recalled, so the
address has to keep resolving. A redirect here fixes both at once, and the
second one matters most: it is read at the moment somebody's deploy has just
broken.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Keep the anchor a heading names for itself
commits.body:
Moving the docs into this repo changed which renderer produces their heading
ids, and the new one derived them from the visible text. The docs write
headings as self-links — `## [Checking deploy status & logs](#status-and-logs)`
— where the href is the anchor every cross-reference points at. Deriving an id
instead meant those links landed at the top of the page rather than the
section, silently.

The explicit slug now wins wherever a heading carries one, for both the
rendered heading and the contents rail, which have to agree.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Require a token for console-initiated deploys
commits.body:
The console's "Deploy an app" prompt told the agent to deploy
anonymously. An anonymous deploy creates the project under an orphan
company (hostnsoft-api projectClaim.ts adopts it only on a later
tokened redeploy), so the app never appeared in the owner's "Your apps"
and was torn down 24h later — the opposite of what clicking Deploy in
your own console promises, and of the empty state's "your app appears
here".

Signed-in copies now instruct the agent to use DEPLOY_TOKEN or
~/.embarko/credentials, and to ask for a token if neither is present,
naming the Deploy tokens page. Anonymous-first is kept for the
marketing pages, where it's the actual pitch.

build() took three positional arguments that no longer distinguished
these cases (console-with-no-app and landing-page both being build("")),
so it now takes a PromptContext object and picks one of four credential
lines.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Lead the copy prompt with the docs, and branch the credential line
commits.body:
The prompt opened with `npx skills add` and a piped install script. Both
are executable code from a domain the agent has never heard of, and
capable agents are trained to refuse that shape: observed with a
customer, the agent declined both paths, spent a turn explaining
supply-chain risk, then fell through to the docs anyway. Lead with the
docs URL instead — fetching a page is the one first move nothing
refuses, and the docs route straight back to the same script under a
fetch-read-run flow, so the skill is still the deploy path.

Then say what to do about credentials, because otherwise the agent
follows the docs' own numbered steps and blocks on obtaining a token
before it has packaged anything. The right answer differs by who is
copying, so build() now picks one of three:

- marketing pages: deploy anonymously, ask for an email only once
  there's a live URL
- tokens page: use the token that's on screen, don't go anonymous
- inside an existing app: that app is claimed, so reach for
  DEPLOY_TOKEN/~/.embarko/credentials

The previous single template told a console redeploy to deploy
anonymously, which cannot update an already-claimed app.

Bundled rather than read from disk because production is a Cloudflare

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Add API keys to the showcase
commits.body:
The best feature in the section was missing, and it is one of the few that
already works: the variables page means an app can talk to Stripe, Resend or
OpenAI with a key the owner saves once and never hands over again. That is
worth more to someone deciding than backups are, so it sits with the shipped

The mockup masks the values the way the console does, so the drawing doesn't

The docs link gets a per-feature label. Lowercasing the rail label for
mid-sentence use produced "See how api keys works" — wrong twice — so the
phrasing drops the verb and the acronym keeps its case.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Mark Login, Files and Backups as upcoming
commits.body:
They were sitting in the middle of the rail described in the present tense,
alongside three features that actually exist. The rail now runs Domain,
Database, Uptime, then the three that don't, each carrying an Upcoming tag —
leading with something the owner can't have yet sells the wrong thing, and
interleaving the two makes them check every row for a tag.

The tag repeats inside the panel, because the mockup under it draws a working
feature and a drawing is persuasive enough to be taken for one. Their copy
moves to the future tense, the docs link goes (there is nothing to read about
an unbuilt feature), and the prompt column's heading becomes "You'll be able
to say" — "Tell your agent" over a feature that doesn't exist is an
instruction that would fail.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Show what's included instead of listing it
commits.body:
The eight-cell grid stated eight facts and stopped there. "Your data is backed
up automatically" is true, and it gives the reader nothing to do with it —
eight cells of that read as a spec sheet, which is the one thing this product
is trying not to be.

The replacement picks one at a time: what it is, a small drawing of it, and
the sentence you would actually say to your agent to get it. That third column
is the argument of the whole section. Every feature here is asked for in words
rather than configured, and printing the words makes that concrete in a way
another paragraph about it could not.

One component across /v1, /v3 and /v4 — they are three palettes over the same
content, so the difference is a `tone` prop rather than three copies of the
markup. The mockups are drawn in divs rather than screenshotted: a screenshot
of the console would be stale by the next release, and at this size the shapes
carry it. /v4's orbit goes too; a ring of labels around the logo described
Embarko's architecture rather than the owner's app.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Offer Apply changes only when something changed
commits.body:
A button that is always there reads as a thing you are supposed to press, and
this one restarts the app. It now appears when a variable is added, edited or
removed, and goes away once the change has been applied. The deploy notice
outlives it, so the confirmation doesn't disappear along with the button that
produced it.

Reading "pending" from the data would survive a reload and was the first
attempt, but a deploy writes its own variables after its record is created, so
every untouched app came out permanently pending and the button never left.
The cost of tracking it in the page instead: an edit left unapplied is
forgotten when the tab closes. Telling the owner that properly needs the API
to say when the running container last took its variables, which the
deployment record cannot answer.

Removing a variable also clears the notice, which otherwise sat there saying
a variable had been saved while the list no longer contained it.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Sit the traffic bars on the bottom of their card
commits.body:
The grid row is as tall as the Top paths card beside it, and the plot area was
a fixed 8rem, so the bars floated in the upper third of the chart with a third
of the card empty beneath the axis labels.

The plot area now takes the slack, which puts the bars on the bottom edge
wherever the row lands. The min-height keeps the old size for the stacked
mobile layout, where nothing stretches the card.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Say what the link opens
commits.body:
"Revoked" on its own, sitting under a table, reads as a column header or a
status rather than a thing to click.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Keep revoked tokens out of the way
commits.body:
A revoked token can't be rotated, revoked again, or used — it is a record, not
something you act on. Six of them were sitting above the tokens that actually
work, greyed out with an empty action column, pushing the live ones down the
page.

The table now lists only tokens that still work, with a Revoked link beneath
it for anyone checking what they took out of service. A token mid-rotation has
a revokedAt in the future and still deploys, so it stays with the live ones
carrying its rotating tag; only a date that has already passed counts as dead.
The revoked table trades the action column for the date it happened, which is
the only thing left worth knowing.

The reveal banner also loses its tint for the standard card surface, and the
empty state stops mentioning CI pipelines.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Name tokens for the owner instead of asking them to
commits.body:
The name field was the loudest thing on a page whose only job is handing over
a credential, and it was optional — so the owners who engaged with it typed
"test" three times, and a name that distinguishes nothing is worse than one
nobody chose.

The button now names the token itself, two calm words like soft-lantern. A
handle beats a description here: the panel cannot know whether a token is
going to Claude Code, to Cursor, or to a build server, so a name claiming to
know would often be wrong. The name only has to survive one moment — the
owner scanning the list deciding which row to revoke — and for that, unique
and memorable is the whole requirement.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Hand over a ready-to-paste prompt, not a bare token
commits.body:
Someone arriving at this page is asking "where do I get a token?", and the
answer used to be a 40-character string they had to work out what to do with.
Now the reveal leads with the deploy prompt with the token already inside it,
so there is one thing to copy and nothing to configure.

The name field was also the loudest thing on the page while being the least
important: optional, capped at 40 characters, and stretched the full width
ahead of the only button that does anything. Size it to its content, label it
properly so the name survives typing, and lock it while the request is in
flight.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Answer the Apply changes button where the button is
commits.body:
The environment page had one notice slot shared by three actions, all
rendering at the top of the page — so pressing Apply changes at the
bottom put its confirmation off-screen above the variables table, where
a reader is entitled to assume nothing happened.

The deploy result now has its own slot, rendered directly above the
button, and the save confirmations stay next to the form that produced
them. Either action clears the other's message so a stale "Deployment
started" cannot outlive the thing it described.

Re-deploy is called Apply changes: it restarts the current image with
the saved variables and rebuilds nothing, which "re-deploy" oversells.
The surrounding copy follows the new name.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Say what app settings do, in the owner's words
commits.body:
The page described itself to an engineer: "Slug (immutable)", "App ID",
"the deployed container keeps running until the backend adds a teardown
step". None of that is the reader's vocabulary, and the slug row showed
the same string as the app name directly above it, so the one fact worth
knowing — the web address — was never stated.

Name and memory now rest as plain values behind a pencil, and each
explains itself only once opened. Settings is somewhere you come to
check what an app is called far more often than to change it, and a page
of open inputs invites edits nobody came to make.

The warning that removal does not take the app offline is kept, in plain
words. An owner who removes an app and later finds the URL still
answering is a support ticket.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Stop v2's tall steps from scrolling out of reach
commits.body:
The step container centred its child with `items-center` while scrolling
with `overflow-y-auto`. A centred flex item that outgrows its container
overflows in both directions, and the half above the top edge cannot be
scrolled to — scrollTop stops at 0. On a 375px screen that put step 1's
headline 77px above the viewport with no way back to it. The hero step
fit, so nothing looked wrong until you advanced.

Auto margins centre when the content fits and collapse when it does not,
which is the behaviour this wants.

The header is fixed and takes no space in the column, so the padding
here is what keeps the first line clear of it. The back button is opaque
now: it floats over a scrolling column, and a 5% tint let the cards read
straight through it.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Make the v1 landing page work on a phone
commits.body:
Two faults, both invisible on a desktop.

The scene arrows are fixed to the bottom centre, so on a narrow screen
they landed on top of the copy — at 375px they overlapped the "Works
with every agent" line. They are pictures of keyboard keys, which a
phone does not have, and the touch handler already advances on swipe,
so they are now hidden below sm rather than repositioned.

The scenes were 100vh. On mobile that is the viewport with the browser
toolbar collapsed, so every scene measured taller than the visible area
and SectionSnap's "has this scene been read to its edge?" guard never
stopped being true — the snap never fired at all. 100dvh measures what
is actually on screen.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: edit env vars option added

commits.author: parakhjain23
commits.subject: Super admin crud support in admin panel

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: env vars update added

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Tell crawlers what to index: sitemap, robots, canonicals
commits.body:
Nothing told a search engine what this site contains. There was no
sitemap and no robots.txt, so /troubleshoot and
/limitations-and-recommendations — linked from nowhere in the site
chrome — had no route into the index at all.

The sitemap builds its doc entries from the DOCS list rather than a
second hand-kept copy, and stays static on purpose: it runs during the
build, where the D1 binding does not exist, so the per-app Showcase
pages are left to be found by crawl from /showcase instead.

robots.txt deliberately does not block /v1../v4. Middleware already
sends those noindex, and a crawler blocked in robots.txt never fetches
the page, so it never reads that header — blocking would have left them
eligible to be indexed as bare URLs while disabling the directive that
actually drops them.

Canonicals come from the root layout, so every page claims its own URL
and a tracking parameter cannot fork it into a competing one.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Render the Showcase pages per request, not at build time
commits.body:
`revalidate` made these static routes, and getCloudflareContext() cannot
run in sync mode in one. The D1 binding only exists inside a request, so
the static export threw and took the whole build down with it — which is
why every new route 404'd in production, /hackathons included, despite
touching no database at all.

force-dynamic instead. These read a live gallery, so per-request is the
honest setting; caching belongs at the edge rather than in a build
artefact that cannot reach the binding anyway.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Add Showcase: the gallery, the submission, and the review queue
commits.body:
Four public routes over one D1 store: /showcase, /showcase/submit,
/showcase/apps/<slug>, and a catch-all for collections
(/showcase/games, /showcase/claude, /showcase/hackathons/<event>).
/submit and /apps are real directories, so Next matches them ahead of
the catch-all and a collection can never shadow them.

The submission form is public and unauthenticated, so approval is the
whole safety model: every public read filters on status = 'approved',
and that filter lives in app/lib/showcase.ts rather than in each page,
because a listing that forgets it publishes spam. Nothing in the request
body can set it. A pending app 404s on its own URL exactly as an unknown
slug does — whether someone's submission was rejected is not this page's
business.

Collection membership is a rule plus a list, unioned: a hackathon
collection picks up anything carrying its code without a join row, and
curated entries are added by hand. That is why hackathons work at all
here — Embarko creating the code and preselecting it at submission time
is backend work that does not exist yet, so the code is an optional
field on the form for now.

The SEO rule is enforced rather than documented: a collection renders…

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Move the contents list to its own rail beside the doc
commits.body:
"On this page" sat under Guides in the left column, which read as one
long menu: moving between documents and moving within one are different
acts, and stacking them made the second look like more of the first. It
also pushed the guides list off a short viewport on the longer docs,
where the contents run to 21 entries.

The rail only appears at xl. Between lg and xl a third column takes its
width out of the prose rather than out of the margin, so below xl the
list stays where it was. That is why TocBlock is a component now — it
renders on whichever side the breakpoint calls for.

Widened the container to max-w-7xl so the prose keeps its measure with
three columns in play. The header and footer set their own widths, so
nothing else shifts.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Publish the hackathons doc
commits.body:
Adds the fourth published doc, hackathons.md, which upstream already
serves. Registering it in DOCS is most of the work: the sidebar switcher
maps over that list, and localizeDocHref uses the slug to rewrite the
doc's links to docs.md into /docs rather than handing the reader a raw
markdown file.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Lead the deploy prompt with what Embarko is, and offer a no-npx path
commits.body:
The prompt now opens with "Embarko is Cloud for small apps." — an agent
that has never heard of Embarko was being asked to deploy to it with no
statement of what it is.

Adds a standalone-script fallback for agents that can't run npx, across
the prompt and the per-tool instruction files. It fetches the byte-
identical script the skill ships, so the fallback can't quietly become a
lesser deploy path than the skill's.

The script's own error output no longer points at SKILL.md and
scripts/troubleshoot.md, which a standalone run doesn't have — it cites
the equivalent URLs instead.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: updated few mds and promt

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Point the re-deploy notice at the deployment, not the version numbers
commits.body:
The notice named the old and new versions, which told the reader nothing
they could act on: after a re-deploy the question is whether it worked,
and that answer lives on the Deployments tab. Link there instead.

The link goes to Deployments rather than the live URL because until the
deploy finishes, that URL is still serving the old app.

The info variant tints the whole banner, which made the sentence read as
one long link and left the real link indistinguishable inside it. Keep
the blue ground and border, and put the colour only on what you click.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Put the admin panel on the console's theme
commits.body:
Admin was a separate design language — hardcoded gray/blue Tailwind, a dark
gray-900 sidebar, blue accents — which is why it could not follow any theme.
Its colours now go through the same tokens as the console: surfaces, text,
borders, the neutral black/white accent, and the status scale.

It gets the same theme script and provider, reading the same stored key, so the
choice made in one panel is the one you get in the other.

Customer queries clip the message to one line. These messages run to full bug
reports, and letting them wrap made a single row a screenful and buried every
column to the right of it; the whole text is a click away in a sheet, matching
the deployments table.

The selected row is tracked by index rather than id because these rows are
allowed to arrive without one, so changing the source filter clears it — the
held index would otherwise point at a different query than the one opened.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Show night skies behind the apps list in dark mode
commits.body:
Three night photos to match the three day ones, self-hosted for the same
reason: the backdrop is part of the product and shouldn't depend on a
third-party host. From Unsplash (free for commercial use, no attribution
required), resized and recompressed to sit alongside the existing skies.

The brightness rule inverts with the theme. The day skies are high-key because
anything darker fights the text over them; on the dark ground it's the light
parts of a photo that fight instead, so these are low-key.

The image also stops being dimmed by opacity. Two dimmers were stacked — a
layer opacity and a gradient painting the page ground back over it — and their
product left the sky at roughly 14% at its strongest, fading to nothing well
before the cards. The gradient alone now does the blending, which is all it was
ever meant to do.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Add light/dark theming to the console
commits.body:
Every Tailwind colour already resolved through a CSS var, so this is a token
swap rather than a component rewrite: the dark palette redeclares the same
names. Status colours are lifted, since the light values sit near 3:1 against
the dark ground and read as muddy.

The preference has three values — light, dark, system — but only the resolved
one (light or dark) is ever written to the DOM, as data-theme on <html>. CSS,
Tailwind's dark: variant and the switcher all read that single attribute, so
they cannot disagree about which theme is showing. darkMode is pointed at the
same attribute; left on the default media strategy, someone on a dark OS who
picks Light would still get dark: variants.

System keeps deferring rather than resolving once: a matchMedia listener means
changing the OS theme changes the console live.

The theme is derived from the preference and the OS state rather than stored
alongside them. Keeping it in its own state meant two effects wrote to it on
mount while the preference was still the default, and the OS watcher landed
last — a saved "dark" came back as light.

An inline script applies the theme before first paint, so there is no flash.
That deliberately makes…

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Open deploy detail and app logs in side sheets
commits.body:
The deployments table grew its detail panel underneath itself, so clicking a
row pushed the page down and moved the row you had just clicked. Detail now
opens in a sheet docked to the right instead.

Both sheets are non-modal and backdrop-free: the table stays live, so clicking
a different row swaps the sheet's contents rather than closing it and making
you click twice. Radix closes a non-modal dialog on any outside interaction,
which would fight exactly that, so interact-outside is prevented and closing is
the X, Esc, or clicking the open row again.

App logs get their own sheet rather than a section inside a deploy's detail.
The endpoint reports the app's current allocation, so the logs are the same
whichever deploy row is selected — hanging them off a row would imply a
per-deploy history that doesn't exist.

That endpoint also needs its own BFF route. It lives on the deploy endpoint's
root, while the generic /api/hns proxy prefixes the management API base, so
routing it through there lands on /api/apps/:slug/logs and 404s.

Fact's `flush` variant kept bg-card while dropping its padding. Inside a Panel
that was invisible (same colour), but on any other surface it drew white boxes…

commits.subject: Hardcode MSG91 widget fallback on connector login page
commits.body:
Matches the existing fallback pattern in LoginModal.tsx and LoginScreen.tsx

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Keep the dev-only Cloudflare hook out of the build
commits.body:
Re-applies the NODE_ENV guard from b740d21, reverted in 01ac604.

`next build` evaluates next.config.mjs too, so the unconditional
initOpenNextCloudflareForDev() opens the wrangler platform proxy during
every production build. DB_ADMIN is `remote: true`, so that means a live
connection to production D1 — fine locally where wrangler is logged in,
fatal in Cloudflare's build sandbox, which has no credentials and loops
on "Establishing remote connection..." until the 30-minute timeout.

A build must not need the database it is being built to talk to.

commits.author: Yogesh Patel
commits.subject: Add AI-connector OAuth login page and same-origin callback bridge
commits.body:
New /connector/login page hosts the MSG91 widget for AI-client (MCP)
logins and forwards proxy_auth_token + the caller's redirect_uri/state
to hostnsoft-api's callback via a same-origin bridge route, since the
browser can't call hostnsoft-api directly. hostnsoft-api's allowlist
and code/state forwarding do the rest.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Restore the unconditional initOpenNextCloudflareForDev() call
commits.body: Reverts the NODE_ENV guard from b740d21, at Ashish's request.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Keep the dev-only Cloudflare hook out of the build
commits.body:
next.config.mjs is evaluated by `next build`, not just `next dev`, so
initOpenNextCloudflareForDev() ran during every production build. With
DB_ADMIN marked `remote: true`, that made the build open a live connection
to production D1 — fine locally, where wrangler is logged in, and fatal in
Cloudflare's build sandbox, which sat on "Establishing remote connection..."
until the 30-minute timeout. Every push since the split-binding change
failed this way while the build itself was perfectly healthy.

A build must not need the database it is being built to talk to.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Make the A/B numbers mean what the dashboard says they mean
commits.body:
Attribution was wrong at the source. trackEvent read the arm from the
lp_variant cookie and fell back to 'v1' -> alpha when there wasn't one,
but middleware only sets that cookie on `/` — so every visitor landing
straight on /v2../v4, and everyone blocking cookies, was filed under
alpha. It also ignored the page being viewed, so a visitor bucketed to
alpha opening /v3 logged a /v3 view as alpha. Resolve path-first and fall
back to the cookie, exactly as the deploy prompt already did, and drop
the event entirely when neither knows rather than guessing. The v1->alpha
mapping it used went with it: the cookie has always held arm names, so
that table only ever worked through its passthrough.

Everything is now counted per visitor rather than per event. One person
clicking Copy three times was three clicks, and CTR could exceed 100%.
That also settles a mismatch the counters had — page views fire on the
four landing pages while the header's login/signup CTAs are site-wide, so
a click could reach the numerator with nothing in the denominator. Rates
are restricted to visitors who saw the arm's landing page, which makes
the numerator a subset by construction.

variant_metrics is no longer w…

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Spell out "Last updated" on the app card

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Show when an app was last updated, not when it was added
commits.body:
The footer read "Added 3d ago · 8 Sept 2026" — the same timestamp twice,
and the wrong one: creation date says nothing about whether an app has
been touched since.

Labelled "Updated" rather than "Deployed" deliberately. updatedAt tracks
the project record, and a rollback changes the running version without
moving it, so it must not be read as a deploy time.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Drop the outline from the app cards
commits.body:
The surface and its shadow already lift a card off the sky; a third edge
on top of those turned a grid of apps into a table. Hover keeps the lift
and the deeper shadow, so nothing is lost by removing the border colour it
used to change.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Close the gap between an app's name and its URL
commits.body:
They are one identity, not two facts, and the card's own gap-3.5 already
separates that block from the row below.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Call a running app "Running"

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Say whether each app is up, in one vocabulary
commits.body:
The apps grid never showed health at all — the thing you open it to find
out — while the app's own page called the same value "Running". The list
endpoint has been returning health, status, currentDeploymentId, createdBy
and updatedAt all along; none were on the Project type, which is why the
card had nothing to show.

HealthPill owns the wording now, in two densities: bare on a card, and a
pill where the overview wants the weight. Six infrastructure values
collapse to three the reader can act on, since nobody responds differently
to "crashed" than to "stopped"; "unknown" stays its own word, because
failing to reach the health service says nothing about the app.

On the card the initial moves left, the way an app icon sits everywhere
else, which frees the top-right for health at a fixed inset — so a grid is
scanned down one column instead of read card by card.

Health is dropped from the shared status vocabulary in format.ts, now that
nothing routes it through StatusPill. Naming these states in two places is
what let the two screens disagree.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Read production metrics in dev without writing to them
commits.body:
The dashboard on localhost showed whatever rows this machine happened to
hold, which answers no question anyone has — you open it to see what real
visitors did.

Bind the same database twice. DB stays local, so browsing the site on
localhost cannot inject page views into the real results: /api/events
writes on every page view, and a remote write binding would corrupt the
very numbers the dashboard exists to report. DB_ADMIN is remote, and the
two admin reads use it. Deployed, both are the same database.

Verified by writing three page views from localhost: local gamma went
1->3 while production stayed at 1 and its event count never moved, and
the dashboard on localhost went on reporting production's figures.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Read isCurrent rather than deducing which deploy is live
commits.body:
The API has always returned isCurrent on every deployment row; it was
just missing from the Deployment interface, so the code believed the
field didn't exist and worked the live deploy out from list order and
status instead. The deduction happened to agree, but a rule inferred from
rollback semantics is a worse thing to depend on than a flag the server
already sends.

Also types updatedAt, returned alongside it and likewise unmodelled.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Mark the running deploy instead of offering to re-run it
commits.body:
"Make this live" sat on the row that already was, reading as though it
would change something when it flips to the same image. The page also
never said which deploy was serving traffic, which is the thing you open
this tab to find out.

The API doesn't mark the live one, which is why every row carried the
button. But it is determinate rather than a guess: the list is newest
first, a failed deploy never takes over from what's running, and a
rollback lands as a brand-new row at the top rather than editing the one
it restores — so the newest successful deploy is live. Every other
successful row keeps its button, so there is still always a way back.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Move the A/B store from better-sqlite3 to D1
commits.body:
The metrics dashboard has never recorded anything in production. The
store was a better-sqlite3 file under DATA_DIR — correct for a Node host,
impossible on Cloudflare, where workerd cannot load a native addon and
there is no writable filesystem to hold the file. Every call threw;
POST /api/events answered 500 while the same request on localhost
answered 200, which is why this survived so long.

D1 is SQLite, so the schema and queries came across unchanged. The
differences: everything is async, the schema moved to migrations/ rather
than being recreated per request (a Worker has nothing to lose between
deploys), and a missing binding now throws instead of leaving an empty
table indistinguishable from no traffic.

next.config.mjs now calls initOpenNextCloudflareForDev() so `next dev`
serves the same binding. That it previously did not is the other half of
the bug: dev and production disagreed about what the database was.

Bindings are typed by a committed cloudflare.d.ts rather than the
gitignored half-megabyte cf-typegen output, which Cloudflare's builder
would not have. Its types come in as inline import() types — a global
reference to @cloudflare/workers-types replaces the DOM's…

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Name the app in the deploy prompt copied from inside it
commits.body:
The prompt left X-App-Name as <name> everywhere. Copied from a project,
that's the one header deciding which app the deploy lands on, and an
unrecognised name creates a new app — so a reader who left the
placeholder got a second copy of their site on a second subdomain.

Pass the slug rather than the display name: the header doubles as the
live subdomain, and the two only match until someone renames one. The
apps list, which has no app yet, still gets the placeholder form.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Drop the blue from the analytics-unavailable note
commits.body:
It isn't a status signal — err/warn/info each ask the reader to react,
and a note explaining why a panel is empty doesn't. Coloured body copy
also reads as a link. Add a neutral `note` variant and use it here, which
keeps the console on the black/white scale.

Its background and border use solid tokens: the palette is var()-based,
so the /10 and /30 alphas the other variants carry silently render
nothing, exactly as the chart bars in ProjectAnalytics already document.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Call the Environment tab "App setup"
commits.body:
The reader is setting up their app and doesn't need to know the platform
files these as environment variables. The page's own heading said
"Environment" too, so the tab and its destination now agree. The route
keeps its name, so no links break.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Give the docs contents list a rail per heading level
commits.body:
Twenty-one entries distinguished only by 12px of indent and 1px of type
size, with nothing marking where the reader currently is. Group the h3s
under their h2 and give each level its own vertical rail — the inner one
starting exactly at the parent's text edge — so nesting reads off the
lines rather than off the indent.

Track the heading the reader is under and ride the active marker on
whichever rail it belongs to. Section labels move off neutral-400, which
was about 2.5:1 at 12px.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Show customer queries from every source behind one filter
commits.body:
The admin split queries across two pages keyed on a hardcoded
'dashboard' | 'public' union, so agent submissions coming in through
ship.embarko.ai landed in the store and were never rendered anywhere.

Read the endpoint unfiltered and derive the filter chips from the sources
actually present in the response, so a route the API starts serving later
appears on its own. Rows with no source group under Unknown rather than
being dropped, and Source/Project/Agent are columns now that the list is
mixed.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Move the documentation from /doc to /docs
commits.body:
The deploy prompt and llms.txt already pointed people at embarko.ai/docs,
which was a 404 — the route had only ever existed in the singular. Rename
the route to match what we publish rather than the other way round, and
redirect /doc permanently so older shared links keep working.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Show per-app analytics, and close the A/B tracking gaps
commits.body:
The Overview page now reads GET /companies/:c/projects/:p/analytics and
renders traffic, latency and resource usage with a range switcher. A 503
from that endpoint says the pipeline is unreachable, which is not the same
as an idle app, so the two states are worded apart rather than both
rendering as zeroes.

The split test was undercounting: v1's second copy button recorded nothing,
and cta_login / cta_signup could never be populated because nothing called
trackCTA for them — wired into the shared header so all four arms report.
The metrics API also sorted arms alphabetically, putting Delta before Gamma.

Also: the brand mark now sits beside the wordmark in the header and footer,
and the admin sidebar stays put while long pages scroll.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Lead the apps page with the deploy prompt itself
commits.body:
Rename the list to "Your apps" and the action to "Deploy an app", and make
the empty state do the job: the prompt is shown inline with a copy icon
instead of hidden behind a dialog, followed by the same numbered run-through
the marketing pages use. That step row now lives in the console kit so v1,
v4 and the console share one wording — "Copy prompt" in every place.

Also carries the in-progress docs rendering, members widget and favicon
asset updates.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Render docs from the published markdown, hand Members to the proxy widget
commits.body:
The docs page kept its own hand-written copy of content that hostnsoft-api
already publishes at /api/public/docs.md, so the two drifted. It now fetches
and renders that markdown instead. The fetch has to happen server-side: the
endpoint only allows CORS from embarko.ai, so the browser can't read it from
any other origin. Cached for five minutes so visitors don't each hit upstream.

Members is now MSG91's user-management widget — the same proxy-auth script
that powers login, mounted with type "user-management" — replacing the
console's own invite form, member table and removal flow. The widget takes the
proxy token as a client-side config field, which is why there's a new
/api/auth/widget-token route: every other path deliberately keeps that token
in an httpOnly cookie, and this is the one place that can't.

Also: wire up the favicon set that was sitting unreferenced in public/assets
(and fix the manifest, whose icon paths pointed at the site root and whose
name was empty), park rename/delete on the company switcher, and centre the
digits in the hero's step markers.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Route customer queries through the API and tighten the admin gate
commits.body:
Customer feedback now goes to hostnsoft-api instead of the local SQLite
file. The public form posts to POST /public/customer-query, and the console
gets a Contact button that posts to POST /companies/:id/customer-query, where
the API reads the email off the verified session. Both offer the same
Feedback | Feature choice as a segmented toggle. contact_messages stays only
so /api/contact/list can still read the rows written before this.

Admin: /admin pages route through a shared requireAdmin() that requires the
isSuperAdmin flag from hostnsoft-api. The previous check accepted any signed-in
user, because its ADMIN_EMAILS allowlist only applies when that variable is
set and it isn't set here — so every logged-in account was being served the
admin shell. Adds the apps and customer-query (dashboard + public) surfaces.

Console header: navigation moves to the left beside the account it belongs to,
Contact and the plan chip sit on the right. Drops the focus ring on the account
menu, which Radix left drawn over the header after every menu close, keeping a
tint so keyboard focus is still visible.

Also carries the sky/atmosphere backdrop work and the CLAUDE.md and
deploy-troubleshooting not…

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Add deploy rollback, bulk env import, and admin/contact surfaces
commits.body:
Console changes:
- Deployments table gains a "Make this live" action per successful deploy,
  wired to POST .../deployments/:id/rollback. Shown on every successful row
  rather than hidden on an inferred-live one: nothing the API returns says
  which deploy is actually serving, and hiding it on a wrong guess would
  remove the only way back.
- Environment gains a Re-deploy button that rolls the newest successful
  deploy back into service, which is how saved variables reach the running
  app without a rebuild.
- Environment gains bulk variable import: paste a block or upload a .env,
  parsed and shown back before saving. No `accept` filter on the file input
  because it matches by extension and ".env" has none.
- Removing a variable now asks first; the value can't be recovered.
- Domain DNS records show Proxy: Disabled, on A records as well as CNAME.
- App cards drop the memory badge and merge the two createdAt rows into one.

Also lands the admin dashboard, contact/events/metrics routes, and the
hero A/B tracking store.

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: web and panle changes

commits.author: Ashish Yadav
commits.subject: Add a Domain section to projects for attaching custom domains
commits.body:
Walks the three steps the API implies: register the domain and show the DNS
record it returns, let the user copy each field to take to their own registrar,
then verify on demand.

Verify's 422 is the expected "DNS hasn't propagated yet" answer rather than a
failure, and its body carries the same domain shape as a success — including
the record to retry against. HnsError now keeps the parsed error body so
domainsApi.verify can resolve for both outcomes, which lets the page render one
flow instead of branching on transport status.

commits.subject: fix(orphan): never let cleanup tear down an app someone just redeployed
commits.body:
Orphan cleanup read its list of expired orphans once, then tore each one
down and deleted its row without checking again. Token adopt and
anonymous redeploy never checked expiry, so an expired orphan waiting
for the next sweep could be adopted or redeployed, and cleanup would then
wipe the new deploy, its data and (after an adopt) a company's project.

- Expired orphans are frozen: token adopt, anonymous redeploy and the
  claim link refuse them with 409 app_expiring. Adopt and the claim link
  check expiry inside the write itself (unexpiredOrphanWhere).
- Cleanup tears down with ifIdle and skips an app whose deploy is still
  in flight on hostnsoft-deploy, retrying on the next run.
- Cleanup's delete only removes a row that is still an expired orphan.

No schema change. Other tearDownApp callers are unchanged.

commits.author: Yogesh Patel
commits.subject: Harden connector redirect: origin-exact matching, HTTPS-only, single-use code
commits.body:
resolveConnectorRedirect previously did a raw startsWith prefix check,
which a redirect_uri like https://partner.com.evil.com could pass against
an allowlist entry of https://partner.com. Now parses both sides and
compares origin + normalized path prefix, and rejects non-HTTPS targets
outright.

The MSG91 callback also no longer puts the live proxy_auth_token in the
redirect URL to the connector - that URL lands in browser history and
plausibly in the receiving service's own access logs, and the PAT is a
long-lived credential, not something scoped to this one handoff. It now
mints a single-use, short-TTL opaque code (connectorPendingLogin.ts,
Redis-backed) and hands that out instead; POST /connector/token redeems
it for the real PAT server-side, once.

commits.author: Yogesh Patel
commits.subject: Add allowlisted redirect support for AI-connector OAuth login
commits.body:
MSG91 callback now recognizes an allowlisted redirect_uri (+ state) and
redirects back to the connector with a standard OAuth `code` param
instead of only supporting the dashboard's own redirect. /connector/token
accepts that code (JSON or form-encoded) alongside the existing `token`
field, and /connector/token/validate gains a GET variant that reads a
Bearer header and answers via HTTP status, matching how a generic
OAuth/API-key proxy validates a stored credential.

An app can now carry an optional embarko.json in its top folder. Today
it holds one setting, "schedules", the app's timed jobs. It is read from
the uploaded archive before the claim, so it works for every upload path
including the connector's JSON files list.

- The schedules go to the API's claim, which validates them and creates

  applied. A failed build never changes them.
- Refused before any work: invalid JSON (with line and column), not an
  object, schedules not a list, over 64 KB, or anything that looks like a
  secret (secrets_in_embarko_json).
- Warnings in the 202, never refusals: file in a subfolder, near-miss
  names like .embarko or embarko.yaml, unknown keys, schedules on a
  static site, and an app that has schedules but sent none this time.
- detect-timers.js: when no schedules are declared, the dependency
  manifests are checked for in-process timer libraries (node-cron,
  APScheduler, rufus-scheduler, robfig/cron...). Those timers stop when
  the app is put to sleep, so the reply warns and quotes any cron
  expressions found in the code.

commits.subject: Let webhooks from HTTP client libraries wake sleeping apps
commits.body:
python-requests, go-http-client, okhttp and java/ were treated as bots,
so a webhook sent by one of them could neither wake a sleeping app nor
keep it awake. Those are exactly the clients other services' backends
send webhooks with, so apps driven by events stayed asleep.

They now count as real traffic. Scanners using them are still caught by
the path patterns when they probe. One that only fetches "/" keeps an app
awake a little longer, which is the cheap direction of this file's bias.

commits.subject: Close the 502 window after a scale-to-zero stop
commits.body:
Since the seed list was retired every wake router sits at priority 1,
below the app's own router. After a stop Traefik keeps that router until
its next Nomad poll, so requests in that window got an instant 502 that
never reached the activator.

stop (and confirms it in the file), the activator holds wakes until the
stop and snapshot finish, and lowers the router back to 1 once the app is
awake. Sleep state is one file per app under .scale-to-zero/sleep/, and
the router file's tmp name is now unique per write since three processes
rewrite it.

commits.author: Vaibhav Mishra
commits.subject: Verify the Docker image exists after the Railpack build before deploying
commits.body:
performBuildAndDeploy treated railpack's exit code 0 as proof that an
image had been built. It is not: a production incident (assetdesk) had
railpack exit 0 with no image under the tag, and the deploy carried on
to `nomad job run`, where the allocation died pulling an image that was
never there. The failure surfaced as a runtime problem far from the
build log that could have explained it.

Add assertImageExists, which runs `docker image inspect <imageName>`
right after the build output is captured and before the data directory,
purgeIfNotRunning and Nomad are touched. A missing image now fails the
deploy through the existing finishDeployFailure path with an error that
names the tag, points at GET /apps/:appName/logs and appends Docker's
own stderr. The captured railpack output is kept, and a running previous
version of the app is never purged over a build that produced nothing.

The root cause of railpack exiting 0 without an image is still unknown;
docs/CLAUDE.md is updated to say the check is in place and where to look
if it recurs.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Accept JSON source on POST /apps for MCP tool deploys
commits.body:
An MCP tool call can only carry JSON, so POST /apps (multipart tarball
only) left agents no way to send code except curling ship.embarko.ai
from their own sandbox, which the sandbox egress policy blocks.

POST /apps now also takes Content-Type: application/json with
{ appName, files: [{ path, content, encoding? }], version? }. The files
are packed into the same tar.gz the multipart path produces and set as
req.file, so the rest of the pipeline is unchanged. Multipart requests
skip the new middleware entirely. Limits: 25 MB body, 2000 files; paths
must be relative with no "..".

commits.author: Parakh Jain
commits.subject: Change a static app's address (#16) (#17)
commits.body:
The rename endpoint only knew the container migration: inspect the Nomad
job, retag images, move the data dir, run a new job. A static app has
none of those — it is a directory under STATIC_SITES_ROOT and a router
file in TRAEFIK_DYNAMIC_DIR — so the jobInspect check reported
app_not_found ("No Nomad job named X") for an app that exists and is
serving. Static apps and the rename shipped in the same week from
different branches, and neither knew about the other.

renameStaticApp is the whole migration for that kind: move the site
directory (the `current` symlink is relative and survives), rename the
manifest, write the new router before removing the old one so some name
answers at every moment, then carry the analytics rows and any
scale-to-zero registry entry, same as the container path. No certificate
wait: the zone wildcard already covers every platform hostname. On any
failure before the old router is removed, the directory moves back and
the old routing was never touched.

The route picks the migration by kind, the same isStaticApp check the
status and config-push endpoints already use.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: scale-to-zero: stop scanners from cold-starting sleeping apps
commits.body:
Step 6's first 24 hours: 19 stops, 9 cold starts, zero failures, and three
aborts that were all the deploy-in-flight guard working. The mechanism is
sound. What the log also showed is that a meaningful share of those wakes
were credential scanners.

  demo-python:          GET /.git/config   served in 5916ms   <- woke it
  scale-to-zero-test-1: GET /.env          served in 3872ms   <- woke it
  pushpendra-agrawal:   GET /htdocs/.env, /psnlink/.env, /tmp/phpinfo.php

Two bugs behind it.

The activator had no bot filter at all. idle-report.js ignores scanner hits
when deciding to STOP, but nothing filtered the decision to WAKE — so an app
slept, a scanner probed /.env, and it burned a cold start and stayed up for
another full idle threshold. It now refuses to cold-start for automated
traffic and answers 404. Only the cold start is refused: a RUNNING app still
serves these normally, since answering differently depending on whether an
app happens to be awake would be a behaviour change its owner never asked
for. A Nomad error while checking falls through to serving, because erring
toward answering a possibly-real user beats erring toward a 404.

SCAN_PATH_PATTERN was anchored at ^/, so…

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: scale-to-zero Step 7: opt in via X-Scale-To-Zero on POST /apps
commits.body:
NOT for prod yet. Step 6's 24h observation window is running, and this
carries a routing change that affects every app on the host — deploying it
mid-window would make tomorrow's read ambiguous about whether any problem
came from the scale-to-zero mechanism or from this.

The allowlist stops being a frozen array and becomes data, which is a real
reduction in the safety rail. Three things compensate: the code seed still
exists and the registry can only ADD to it; opting in requires an
authenticated deploy FOR THAT APP, so there is no endpoint that adds an
arbitrary name; and being listed only means "may be considered" —
idle-report still re-checks image, saved spec and DATA_DIR before every
single stop, and the registry cannot waive any of them.

Traefik moves from a single-file to a directory provider. server-setup.sh
owns platform.yml in that directory, deploy-service owns scale-to-zero.yml
and rewrites it in full from the registry, and Traefik hot-reloads it. That
is the only way an app can opt in without a re-provision: dynamic.yml is
generated before the repo is even pulled.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: scale-to-zero Step 4: wake-on-request activator
commits.body:
A stopped app has no Traefik router at all — app routers are generated by
the Nomad provider from RUNNING services — so its hostname 404s rather
than waking anything. activator.js is what a per-app fallback router in
/opt/traefik/dynamic.yml points at: it starts the job from the spec saved
in Step 3, waits for it, and forwards the original request, so a visitor
sees a slow response instead of an error.

The fallback router sits at priority 1. App routers set no explicit
priority, so Traefik derives theirs from rule length (~44 for a Host
rule); a running app outranks the fallback by a wide margin and its
traffic never reaches this process. One router per exact hostname rather
than a wildcard, so "no other app's traffic can reach the activator" is a
property of the config file, not a hope about this code.

Its own pm2 process rather than a route inside deploy-service: it holds
visitor connections open for the length of a cold start, and must not be
able to take the deploy API down with it.

The data-integrity check runs BEFORE nomad job run, not after. An app
that wakes to a missing database does not crash — it creates a fresh one
and reports itself healthy. After the start the app…

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: scale-to-zero: Step 3 verified in prod
commits.body:
A real --apply run against 31 running apps stopped exactly one: 22 other
idle apps were listed under "Idle but NOT stoppable" and left running,
which is the safety rail actually doing work rather than being trivially
satisfied by there being nothing else to stop. nomad job status shows
scale-to-zero-test-1 as "dead (stopped)" — registered, not purged — and
every other app still running.

Worth recording from the manifest: visits.db was 4,096 bytes and
visits.db-wal was 1,001,192. Nearly all the data was in the write-ahead
log, unwritten to the main file, because the container is killed rather
than shut down cleanly. Anything that persisted only the .db file would
have reported success and silently lost the lot.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: scale-to-zero: save a stopped app's job spec so it stays wakeable
commits.body:
Nomad's job_gc_threshold (4h) collects a STOPPED job out of Nomad's
state, and that state was the only place an app's job spec existed:
server.js renders each spec into a temp build directory, runs it, and
deletes the file. So a scaled-to-zero app could only be woken within 4
hours of being stopped, after which the spec was gone for good — nothing
for Step 4's activator to run, and no recovery short of a fresh deploy
from source. It would have failed silently and only on the wake path,
which is exactly the case this plan exists to prevent.

idle-report.js now captures `nomad job inspect` output to
$APP_DATA_ROOT/.specs/<appName>.json BEFORE stopping, and aborts the stop
if the capture fails or returns no matching Job — an app we cannot prove
we can restart must not be stopped. inspect emits {"Job": {...}}, which
`nomad job run -json` accepts back unchanged.

server.js's delete endpoint removes the saved spec alongside the data
directory. A spec surviving a deleted app is not clutter: it is a
complete runnable description of an app the user asked us to remove,
sitting where the activator will look.

Step 0's GC verification box updated accordingly — the re-run has to come
from the s…

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: docs: move scale-to-zero plan into the repo, with per-step progress
commits.body:
The plan was living in a local docs/ folder that is not a git repository,
so "which step are we on" existed only in someone's memory. It is the one
piece of state in this project that must not be lost, since the plan's
whole rule is that a step does not start until the previous one is
verified — and that ordering is worthless if the record of what was
verified disappears.

Now in the deploy-service repo on the deployed branch: adds a Progress
table, a status paragraph under each step saying what was actually
proven rather than merely shipped, and ticks the checklist boxes that
real verification runs have already covered.

Step 3 is explicitly "code shipped, NOT yet verified" — idle-report.js
--apply is deployed and its safety rail demonstrably held (19 idle apps
reported, 0 stopped), but the test app has never actually been stopped,
so the stop/snapshot/manifest path is unexercised.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Fix WASM apps failing with CompileError: add security-headers Traefik middleware
commits.body:
Every app's router (default + custom domains) now gets a Content-
Security-Policy set at the edge via a Traefik headers middleware,
correcting Railpack's own static-site default (missing
'wasm-unsafe-eval' in script-src, which breaks Godot/Unity/Emscripten/
Rust-wasm exports with a CompileError and a blank page — those builds
have no package.json, so Railpack serves them with its own Caddy
default, which this platform previously passed through unmodified).
Traefik's headers middleware replaces a same-name header from the
backend rather than duplicating it, so this can't produce two CSP
headers whose policies get intersected by the browser.

Takes effect on an app's next deploy/rollback/config-push, same as
every other job-spec change — an already-running WASM app needs a
redeploy (or a no-op rollback) to pick it up.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Fix false-positive window.storage detection on docs/comments
commits.body:
grep -rlF matched the literal string anywhere in a file, flagging
pages that merely describe the window.storage rule (docs, comments,
JSX text) as if they used the banned API, blocking legitimate deploys.

Each grep candidate is now confirmed via AST parsing (@babel/parser +
traverse) for a real window.storage MemberExpression, which comments,
strings, and JSX text can never produce. Unparseable/unreadable files
still fail closed (treated as a hit), same as before.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Make POST /apps respond immediately; add status/logs check-back URLs
commits.body:
The build (railpack) + Nomad deploy could take long enough that
Cloudflare's own proxy timeout (524) fired before the deploy had a
chance to finish. POST /apps now does the fast synchronous part (auth,
app-name claim, extraction, window.storage rejection, memory calc)
and responds 202 Accepted immediately with a clear "building in the
background" message plus statusUrl/logsUrl (also mirrored inside the
orphan block for orphan deploys) — the actual build/deploy continues
unawaited in performBuildAndDeploy.

New GET /apps/:appName/status and .../logs, both public and
authenticated the same way as POST /apps itself (Authorization:
Bearer <DEPLOY_TOKEN>, or no header at all — but ONLY while the app is
still an unclaimed orphan; a claimed app requires its owning company's
token, checked live against hostnsoft-api on every request via the new
read-only project-lookup.js, never cached from deploy time). A wrong
company's token gets 404, not the real data, matching the "never
confirm existence to a non-owner" convention used elsewhere.

  uniformly for orphan and token-based deploys, since orphans have no
  company to per…

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Fix analytics subsystems not fully respecting "disabled" when unconfigured
commits.body:
resource-poller.js and retention.js never checked ANALYTICS_DB_PATH
before starting, unlike access-log-tailer.js's own check for
TRAEFIK_ACCESS_LOG_PATH — with analytics meant to be off (both unset),
they'd still spin up, do real work each tick, and only then fail
calling getDb(), logging the same error forever. All three now share
one isAnalyticsEnabled() guard and no-op cleanly with a single warning.

Also floors ANALYTICS_RETENTION_DAYS at 1 — a misconfigured 0 or
negative value would otherwise prune every row on the very next run.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Add per-app traffic and CPU/memory analytics
commits.body:
New analytics/ module: access-log-tailer.js follows Traefik's JSON
access log and attributes each request to an app by its router name;
resource-poller.js samples CPU/memory straight from Nomad's stats API;
query.js serves percentile latency, status-code breakdown, top paths,
and time-bucketed series over 24h/7d/30d/90d/all; retention.js prunes
rows past 100 days. Backed by node:sqlite (no new dependency). New
endpoint: GET /internal/apps/:appName/analytics.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Isolate orphan banner in Shadow DOM, move it to the top
commits.body:
Some client apps' own dark-theme CSS (broad selectors, !important
rules, or CSS custom properties) was cascading into the banner's inline
styles and making its text invisible. A shadow root's stylesheet is a
separate scope no outer page selector can reach into, so this makes the
banner's appearance immune to whatever the hosted app's own CSS does.
Falls back to the old unisolated approach only when attachShadow isn't
available. Also repositioned from bottom:0 to top:0 per request.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Add project health status endpoint backed by real Nomad allocation state
commits.body:
GET /internal/apps/:appName/status parses `nomad job status` output into
a simplified running/crashed/starting/stopped/not_deployed/unknown enum,
replacing hostnsoft-api's previously hardcoded health: "unknown".

Also fixes the orphan-teardown endpoint's not-found detection: Nomad's
actual message is `No job(s) with prefix or id "x" found`, which never
matched the old /not found/i check, so tearing down an orphan whose
deploy had failed (no Nomad job ever created) 500'd instead of
succeeding.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Actually use the project's configured memoryMb during deploy
commits.body:
hostnsoft-api already returned memoryMb from /internal/projects/claim,
but claim-project.js dropped it and server.js's auto-detected 256/512
always won regardless of what was configured. Now takes the configured
value as a floor-adjustable override: Math.max(autoDetectedMinimum,
configured) so a lower configured value can never undercut what an
embedded-DB app actually needs (would OOM), while a higher configured
value is honored.

commits.author: Priyanka P
commits.subject: Bake project env vars into the Nomad job spec
commits.body:
Renders each project's configured env vars into the "server" task's
env block on every deploy and every custom-domain config-push, so they
actually reach the running container instead of only living in
hostnsoft-api's DB. Reserved platform keys (PORT/APP_NAME/APP_VERSION/
DATA_DIR) are dropped rather than overridable. Values are escaped for
safe HCL string embedding, including neutralizing "${" so a value can
never be misinterpreted as Nomad's own interpolation syntax; keys are
re-validated as safe identifiers here too, since an unrestricted key
would be a real job-spec injection vector (it's embedded as a bare
unquoted attribute name).
